newsitem.title: FRANCE: France rejects separatist demands on Comoros.
newsitem.headline: France rejects separatist demands on Comoros.

text.p: France on Monday rejected demands from separatists on impoverished Anjouan island in the Comoros group to return to French colonial rule, saying any solution to the crisis should respect the Indian Ocean archipelago's integrity.

Eager not to set a precedent infringing the inviolability of African borders, Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux voiced hopes that the Comoros government could find solutions to Anjouan's social and economic problems through dialogue.
"Any solution must, quite obviously, fully respect the territorial integrity of the Comoros Islamic Federal Republic. We have already said that we condemn separatist moves," he told a news briefing.
Doutriaux said the Organisation of African Unity would probably have to step in if the crisis continued.

Thousands of protesters demonstrated on Anjouan on Sunday in favour of a return to French rule after President Mohamed Taki asked the islanders to submit proposals for ending a constitutional crisis caused by their demand for secession.
Doutriaux said Taki had proposed a national development plan including improved decentralisation to try to resolve the crisis.
The islanders say they have experienced only poverty and political unrest since the main group of the Comoros islands in the Indian Ocean declared independence from France in 1975.
Anjouan's poverty contrasts with the comparative prosperity of the adjoining island of Mayotte, which voted to remain French in 1975.

The separatist demonstration follows French moves to take a lower profile in Africa after suffering a series of setbacks, including the downfall of its long-time ally Mobutu Sese Seko in Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Defence Minister Alain Richard, confirming plans to cut French troops in Africa to fewer than 6,000 from 8,100, said in an interview with the French daily Liberation on Monday that Paris would avoid intervening in the domestic policies of its former colonies.
